title: What is Python
desc: Python is a programming language people use to write programs in plain-looking text, from small practice scripts to larger apps. You write code in a file or an editor, and a Python program on your computer runs it. It's known for being readable, which is why many beginners start there.

title: Running a Python file
desc: To run a Python file, you need Python installed, then you run the file from an editor or a terminal with a command like python and the filename, depending on your system. Save the file first, watch the error message if it fails, and make sure you're in the folder that actually holds the file.

title: Comments in code
desc: A comment is a note in your code that the program ignores when it runs. In Python, a short comment starts with #. Use comments to explain why something is there, not to repeat what the line already says, and keep them up to date if you change the code.
prompts: what is a comment in code

title: Booleans
desc: A Boolean is a value that is only True or False. Programs use Booleans in conditions, like whether a password matches or a loop should keep going. In Python, True and False start with a capital letter, and comparisons such as == and < produce Boolean results.

title: Elif and else
desc: After an if, elif means 'else if' and tests another condition when the first one wasn't true. else runs when none of the conditions above it were true. Only one branch in that chain runs. Keep the conditions in a sensible order so a later check isn't hidden by an earlier one.
prompts: how does else work in Python

title: Tuples
desc: A tuple in Python is an ordered collection written in parentheses, like (1, 2, 3). It's like a list in that you can index it, but you don't change its items after you make it. Tuples are handy for a fixed pair or a function that returns more than one value.
prompts: what is a tuple in Python

title: Sets in Python
desc: A set in Python is a collection of unique items, written with curly braces, and it doesn't keep a fixed order you should rely on like a list does. Sets are useful when you care about membership or removing duplicates. You can do unions and intersections once you're comfortable with the basics.
prompts: what is a set in Python
help me with sets in Python

title: F-strings
desc: An f-string is a Python way to put values inside a string. You put f before the quotes and write variables in curly braces, like f"Hi, {name}". It's often clearer than stitching strings together with plus signs. The code inside the braces is evaluated when that line runs.
prompts: put a variable in a string in Python

title: String slicing
desc: Slicing lets you take part of a string (or a list) with square brackets, like text[0:3], which starts at index 0 and stops before 3. Leaving a side blank means 'from the start' or 'to the end,' and a negative index counts from the end. Practice with a short word so the numbers make sense.
prompts: how does slicing work in Python

title: Using len
desc: len() tells you how many items are in a string, list, or other sized collection. len("hi") is 2, and len([]) is 0. It's useful in loops and checks, and it counts items, not the last index, so the last index of a list of five items is 4.

title: Syntax errors
desc: A syntax error means Python couldn't even parse the file: a missing colon, a typo, an unclosed quote, or a wrong indent. The message usually points to a line near the problem. Fix the first syntax error, then run again; later messages may be leftovers from the first typo.

title: Type errors
desc: A TypeError in Python means you used a value in a way that type doesn't support, like adding a number to a string without converting, or calling something that isn't a function. Read the message for the types it names, then convert or change the operation. Print the value and its type if you're stuck.

title: Importing a module
desc: import brings in a module of ready-made tools, like import math or import random, so you don't have to write those functions yourself. Import at the top, then use the module name, such as math.sqrt. If the import fails, check the spelling and that the package is actually installed when it's not part of the built-in library.

title: The random module
desc: Python's random module can pick a random integer, shuffle a list, or choose an item, after you import random. It's fine for games and practice, but not for serious security or passwords. If you need the same results while testing, look up random.seed once you know the basics.

desc: try and except let you handle an error that might happen, such as bad input, without crashing the whole program. Put the risky lines in try, and in except decide what to do, like print a clear message and try again. Don't hide every error with a bare except; that makes real bugs harder to see.

title: Parameters and arguments
desc: Parameters are the names you list in a function definition; arguments are the values you pass when you call it. Inside the function, you use the parameter names. Keep the order straight, and start with a small function that takes one or two inputs so it's easier to test.
